content: Karen Ann Quinlan, born on March 29, 1954, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, became a pivotal figure in the history of the right-to-die debate in the United States. At the age of 21, she fell unconscious after returning home from a party and subsequently entered a persistent vegetative state. Despite being kept alive on a ventilator for several months without any signs of improvement, her parents requested that the hospital discontinue active care and allow her to die. The hospital refused, leading to a highly publicized legal battle that set significant legal precedents. The case was groundbreaking not only for its legal implications but also for its appeal to religious principles, as Karen and her family were devout Catholics. Catholic moral theology played a critical role in the case, influencing American law and bioethics globally. Karen was removed from active life support in 1976 but continued to live in a coma for nearly a decade until her death from pneumonia in 1985. Her case continues to raise profound questions in moral theology, bioethics, euthanasia, legal guardianship, and civil rights, profoundly impacting medical and legal practices worldwide. Three major outcomes of her case included the establishment of formal ethics committees in healthcare institutions and the development of advance health directives. Karen Ann Quinlan was adopted as an infant by Joseph and Julia Quinlan, devout Roman Catholics living in Landing, New Jersey. She grew up in a stable family environment with two younger siblings. Some friends described her as living a reckless lifestyle, including alleged drug use, though evidence of this remains contradictory, and her parents denied such claims. In April 1975, shortly after her 21st birthday, Karen moved out of her parents' home and began living with two roommates. Around this time, she embarked on a radical diet, reportedly to fit into a dress she had purchased. On April 15, 1975, after attending a friend’s birthday party at a local bar, she consumed gin and tonics and a tranquilizer, believed to be phenobarbital, Valium, or methaqualone. She had eaten almost nothing for 48 hours. Karen suddenly felt faint, was taken home, and put to bed. When friends checked on her 15 minutes later, they found she was not breathing. Emergency resuscitation efforts restored some color to her skin, but she never regained consciousness. She was admitted to Newton Memorial Hospital in a coma and later transferred to St. Clare’s Hospital. Karen had suffered irreversible brain damage due to a prolonged period of respiratory failure, lasting no more than 15–20 minutes. The exact cause of her respiratory failure remains unclear, though it was speculated that she aspirated on her vomit after passing out. Her eyes were disconjugate, meaning they no longer moved in the same direction, and her EEG showed only abnormal slow-wave activity. She was diagnosed with a persistent vegetative state, a deep and irreversible form of unconsciousness. Over the following months, her condition deteriorated further, with significant weight loss and unpredictable, violent limb movements. She was sustained only by nasogastric feeding and a ventilator. After months of witnessing her unchanging condition, Karen’s family concluded that she was beyond hope and decided to remove her from the ventilator. The hospital refused, likely due to concerns about legal repercussions and the broader societal debate surrounding the right to life. The Quinlan family persisted and, in 1976, took their case to the New Jersey Supreme Court, which ruled in their favor. When Karen was removed from the ventilator, she surprised many by continuing to breathe unaided. She was sustained by artificial nutrition for nine more years until her death. Karen Ann Quinlan remained in a persistent vegetative state until her death from pneumonia in 1985. She was buried at Gate of Heaven Cemetery in East Hanover, New Jersey. At the time of the legal proceedings, Karen’s father, Joseph Quinlan, was assigned legal guardianship by a New Jersey court. His Catholic faith was considered positively in the decision, as Karen herself was Catholic. This brought Catholic moral theology into the case as a relevant factor. The New Jersey Supreme Court’s decision extensively referenced an address by Pope Pius XII to medical professionals on the preservation of life. Catholic moral theology does not require the use of extraordinary means to preserve life, defined as any procedure that imposes an undue burden on the patient, family, or others and goes beyond basic care necessary for sustaining life and dignity, such as food, water, air, and hygiene. A patient has the right to refuse extraordinary means of treatment, even if this hastens natural death. This principle was central to the Quinlan family’s request to remove Karen from the ventilator, and the court honored this principle in its ruling. The case had a lasting legacy, leading to the development of formal ethics committees in hospitals, nursing homes, and hospices, as well as the creation of advance health directives. An autopsy conducted after Karen’s death revealed that while her cerebral cortex had moderate scarring, her thalamus was extensively and bilaterally damaged. Her brainstem, which controls breathing and cardiac functions, was undamaged. These findings suggest that the thalamus plays a particularly important role in consciousness. Karen Ann Quinlan’s case also had a cultural impact. A TV movie was made about her life, with Piper Laurie and Brian Keith portraying her parents. The 1981 film The Verdict, starring Paul Newman, was inspired by her case, though it focused on medical negligence. The term Karen Ann Quinlan cocktail is sometimes jokingly used to refer to the combination of sedatives and alcohol, though such references trivialize the gravity of her story.
